headline: Saudi Construction Chemicals Producers Are Moving Closer to the Projects
deck: Admixtures, waterproofing and repair systems are made in the Kingdom by companies most buyers meet only through a distributor. The specification is now doing the introducing.
excerpt: Construction chemicals are one of the deeper parts of Saudi Arabia's domestic materials base, with CMCI manufacturing in Dammam since 1984 alongside Arkaz and Henkel Polybit. Tighter code requirements and local content rules are pulling those producers into direct contact with contractors.
content:
Construction chemicals are the part of a building nobody photographs. Admixtures that make a mix pumpable in forty-five degree heat, waterproofing membranes under a raft, curing compounds, grouts, sealants, repair mortars and protective coatings rarely appear in a project description, and they account for a small share of the contract value. They also account for a disproportionate share of the defects, because almost every early-life failure in a Gulf building traces back to water, chloride or a joint.

Saudi Arabia manufactures more of this category than most people assume. Construction Material Chemical Industries, CMCI, has produced concrete chemicals from Dammam since 1984 and reports supplying more than 300,000 tonnes of product into over 3,000 projects across the Kingdom and the wider Gulf, with offices in Dammam, Riyadh, Jeddah, Medina, Yanbu, Jubail, Al Hassa and Khamis Mushayt. Arkaz, founded in 2008, has built a specialty building materials and construction chemicals business across the Gulf. Henkel Polybit manufactures waterproofing and construction chemicals with plants in both Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. The multinationals — BASF and Sika among them — sit alongside rather than above these producers in the Saudi market.

Two forces are pulling that domestic capacity into closer contact with the projects. The first is the code. The 2024 edition of the Saudi Building Code became mandatory on 30 June 2025, and its concrete, structural and general modules push the burden of proof onto documented product performance rather than the design team's judgement. Chemicals are unusually exposed to that shift, because their performance is only observable through testing: nobody can look at a cured slab and see whether the admixture dosage was right.

The second is procurement. The Local Content and Government Procurement Authority has been phasing in higher minimum local content percentages for products on the mandatory list used by government buyers, and the Made in Saudi programme requires added value of at least 40 percent for its label. Construction chemicals are well suited to localisation on the industrial logic alone: the products are heavy, often water-based, temperature-sensitive in transit and consumed continuously across a national footprint, which makes long-distance supply expensive and slow.

The practical consequence on a site is about the technical service rather than the drum. A ready-mix supplier adjusting a mix design for a summer pour, a contractor investigating a leaking basement, or an engineer specifying a repair to chloride-damaged reinforcement all need a chemist who will attend, test and sign. That is a service business with a factory attached, and it is one of the reasons the category has resisted import competition in the Gulf far more successfully than, say, control systems or engineered panels.

The distribution layer reinforces the point. Masdar, the Al-Muhaidib building materials business founded in 1971, carries chemicals and adhesives alongside steel, timber and plumbing across more than a hundred branches in 29 cities, which means a specified product can be executed nationally rather than city by city. For a manufacturer, national availability is what turns a project approval into a standing specification.

Where the domestic industry is more exposed is upstream. Polymer dispersions, specialised resins and some active chemistries are imported, and the Kingdom's shift from refining into petrochemicals is only slowly producing the specialty intermediates this sector uses. A local content requirement that reaches the finished pail without addressing the chemistry inside it moves the import one step up the chain, which is a familiar limitation of percentage-based instruments.

For buyers at Big 5 Construct Saudi this week, the questions that separate suppliers in this category are the dull ones: test certificates against the relevant Saudi Building Code module, performance data at Gulf summer temperatures rather than laboratory conditions, shelf life and site storage requirements, compatibility with the concrete mix actually being supplied, and whether a technical representative will attend the first pour. The products themselves are largely commodity chemistry. What is being bought is the assurance around them.
